name: AI/ML as Emerging GPT
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: AI Passed the Same Test the Internet Passed
lesson.summary: Economists use three tests to identify a true general purpose technology: broad applicability, sustained improvement, and the ability to spark further innovation, and artificial intelligence and machine learning currently pass all three, which is exactly why they make a useful comparison point for quantum computing.
lesson.body:
Not every impressive new technology reshapes an economy, and economists have spent decades trying to figure out what separates the ones that do from the ones that stay niche. The framework most commonly used, associated with economists including Timothy Bresnahan and Manuel Trajtenberg writing in the 1990s, identifies a small set of technologies as general purpose: the steam engine, electricity, the internal combustion engine, and modern computing among them. A general purpose technology is judged against three criteria: it must be broadly applicable across many sectors, it must improve over time rather than stay static, and it must enable new complementary innovations built on top of it.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning clear the first test comfortably. The same underlying methods show up in medical imaging diagnostics, warehouse and delivery routing, fraud detection in banking, machine translation, software development tools, scientific research pipelines, and consumer products used by billions of people. This is not one industry adopting one tool, it is a horizontal capability that different sectors are independently finding uses for, which is precisely the pattern that historical general purpose technologies like electricity displayed as they spread from lighting into manufacturing, transportation, and eventually almost every corner of economic life.

The second test, improvement over time, is also visible and measurable. The cost of a given level of model capability has fallen substantially over a period of a few years, benchmark performance on a wide range of tasks has risen consistently across model generations, and capabilities that required specialized infrastructure recently now run on widely available hardware. This mirrors the trajectory of earlier general purpose technologies, where the cost of generating electricity or the density of transistors on a chip fell steadily over long stretches of time, making the technology progressively more useful to more people.

The third test, enabling new complementary innovations, is where the case becomes strongest. Genuinely new products and workflows have formed on top of these systems rather than merely alongside them: recommendation systems that reorganized how people discover media, coding assistants that changed day to day software development practice, and computational biology tools like protein structure prediction that opened new avenues of scientific research. Whole categories of businesses now exist that simply did not have a reason to exist before, built specifically to sit on top of this capability, which is the innovational complementarity that historical general purpose technologies reliably produce.

None of this means every dollar invested in AI and machine learning companies is well spent, or that the field is free of hype, overpromising, and inevitable disappointments along the way, echoes of the dot-com pattern discussed earlier are entirely plausible here too. But the underlying technology itself clears the bar that economists use to identify technologies with economy-wide impact, on all three counts, not just one. That matters because the next chapter applies the exact same three tests, point by point, to quantum computing, and the results look nothing alike.
